# Purpose

This notebook runs and compares population-size estimation methodologies using
the simulated data created in `simulation_data.qmd`. Estimation methods receive
only the observed capture histories; the full simulated data are used after
estimation to evaluate bias, uncertainty, and coverage.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
devtools::load_all("..", quiet = TRUE)
```

# Setup

```{r libraries, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Load Simulation Data

Load the saved full-population scenario data and establish the objects shared by
the estimation workflows. Keep the full records available only for evaluation,
not as estimator inputs.

```{r load-simulation-data}
data_directory_candidates <- c(
    file.path("..", "..", "data"),
    file.path("..", "data"),
    "data"
)
data_directory <- data_directory_candidates[
    vapply(data_directory_candidates, dir.exists, logical(1))
][[1]]
scenario_data <- readRDS(file.path(data_directory, "scenario_data.rds"))
```

# Combine Capture List Groups

Create every unique partition of the six capture columns into complementary
three-column groups. A grouped list is positive when any of its source lists
captured the individual.

## Setup the Capture Groups

The first step to building the capture groups is to identify what the capture
patterns should be. This means we must generate all unique combinations of the
capture columns into two complementary groups of equal size. We start by setting
the number of capture columns, number of columns per group, and the capture
column names. After this, we generate all combinations of the capture columns
into two complementary groups, ensuring the first group always contains
`capture_1` to avoid duplicate groupings. In the case of 6 columns separated
into groups of 3 this produces the following:

| Group 1 | Group 2 |
|---------|---------|
| 1+2+3   | 4+5+6   |
| 1+2+4   | 3+5+6   |
| 1+2+5   | 3+4+6   |
| 1+2+6   | 3+4+5   |
| 1+3+4   | 2+5+6   |
| 1+3+5   | 2+4+6   |
| 1+3+6   | 2+4+5   |
| 1+4+5   | 2+3+6   |
| 1+4+6   | 2+3+5   |
| 1+5+6   | 2+3+4   |

Each group of capture columns is stored as a list containing two elements:
`capture_1` and `capture_2`, each representing one of the complementary groups.
The names are then given a shorthand name based on the indices of the capture
columns.

```{r combine-capture-lists}
n_capture_cols <- 6
n_cols_per_group <- as.integer(n_capture_cols / 2)

capture_columns <- paste0("capture_", seq_len(n_capture_cols))

capture_list_groups <- Filter(
    function(group) {
        return("capture_1" %in% group)
    },
    combn(capture_columns, n_cols_per_group, simplify = FALSE)
) |>
    lapply(function(first_group) {
        return(list(
            capture_1 = first_group,
            capture_2 = setdiff(capture_columns, first_group)
        ))
    })

# Creating the combination names
capture_list_group_names <- vapply(
    capture_list_groups,
    function(groups) {
        paste(
            paste(
                sub("capture_", "", groups$capture_1, fixed = TRUE),
                collapse = "+"
            ),
            paste(
                sub("capture_", "", groups$capture_2, fixed = TRUE),
                collapse = "+"
            ),
            sep = ","
        )
    },
    character(1)
)
names(capture_list_groups) <- capture_list_group_names
```

## Combine the Capture Lists

Now generated, we must combine the data into the group capture lists. This
involves iterating through the full data, identifying whether a person is
captured by one or more of the columns in group 1 or group 2, and then creating
a new column indicating capture in the group.

```{r}
# `capture_groups` is a named list of 2 lists. The name usually follows the
# format "1+2+3,4+5+6" indicating the capture columns in each group. The 2
# sub-lists are named `capture_1` and `capture_2` representing the two
# complementary groups.
#
# Example:
# > capture_groups
# $`1+2+3,4+5+6`
# $`1+2+3,4+5+6`$capture_1
# [1] "capture_1" "capture_2" "capture_3"
# $`1+2+3,4+5+6`$capture_2
# [1] "capture_4" "capture_5" "capture_6"

combine_capture_lists <- function(data, capture_groups) {
    source_columns <- unlist(capture_groups, use.names = FALSE)

    # Get the covariate columns
    combined <- data[setdiff(names(data), source_columns)]

    # Combine the capture columns into the new grouped columns
    # An example group_name: "1+2+3,4+5+6"
    for (group_name in names(capture_groups)) {
        combined[[group_name]] <- as.integer(
            rowSums(data[capture_groups[[group_name]]]) > 0
        )
    }
    return(combined)
}

# Loop through each scenario and combine the capture lists
combined_scenario_data <- lapply(
    scenario_data,
    function(data) {
        return(lapply(
            capture_list_groups,
            combine_capture_lists,
            data = data$full_data
        ))
    }
)
```

# Single-Simulation Estimation

Describe the boundary between estimator inputs and simulation data. For each
scenario, estimators should receive only the observed union and its capture
columns. The full population is retained for evaluation.

## Doubly Robust Methods (Plug-In, TMLE, DR)

Run the initial population-size estimation method for each saved scenario and
capture-list pair. Preserve the scenario metadata and known population counts
alongside each estimate. This consists of looping across each scenario and each
capture-list group within that scenario to build an estimation.

```{r single-simulation-estimates-dr}
# Loop over the scenarios: `mid_capture`, `low_capture`, etc.
scenario_estimations <- lapply(names(scenario_data), function(scenario_name) {
    # loop over the groups: `1+2+3,4+5+6`, `1+2+4,3+5+6`, etc.
    bind_rows(lapply(names(capture_list_groups), function(group_name) {
        estimation_data <- combined_scenario_data[[scenario_name]][[group_name]]
        capture_columns <- get_capture_cols(estimation_data)
        observed <- get_observed_data(estimation_data, capture_columns)
        estimates <- estimate_n(
            observed,
            n_capture_cols = 2,
            estimator_variant = doubly_robust_estimator(
                estimator_func = "logit",
                n_folds = 5,
                margin = 0.05
            )
        )
        return(estimates)
    }))
})

scenario_estimations
```


## Process the Scenario Estimates

After calculating the estimates for each scenario and group, we need to process
all the groups so that they produce a single estimate for each scenario. The 
average estimate is valid because each capture group provides an independent
view of the same pre-captured population population. The minimum of the lower 
confidence interval and maximum of the upper confidence interval is valid
because it ensures that the combined confidence interval covers the true
population size across all independent capture groups.

```{r process-estimates}
averaged <- lapply(scenario_estimations, function(scenario) {
    est <- dplyr::group_by(scenario, method) |>
        dplyr::summarize(
            avg_n = mean(n, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_cil = min(cin.l, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_ciu = max(cin.u, na.rm = TRUE)
        )
    return(est)
})

names(averaged) <- names(combined_scenario_data)
averaged <- bind_rows(averaged, .id = "scenario")

averaged
```

## Log Linear Methods

Log-linear models have a long history of being used to estimate population
sizes. The idea is straightforward, fit a generalized linear model (GLM) to the
observed capture histories and estimate the unobserved portion of the
population. Then add this estimate to the observed count to get the total
population. In this case, we select the best model via the lowest AIC.

```{r single-simulation-estimates-ll}
scenario_estimations_ll <- lapply(
    names(scenario_data),
    function(scenario_name) {
        full_data <- scenario_data[[scenario_name]]$full_data
        n_total <- nrow(full_data)
        bind_rows(lapply(names(capture_list_groups), function(group_name) {
            estimation_data <- create_contingency_table(
                combined_scenario_data[[scenario_name]][[group_name]]
            )
            capture_columns <- get_capture_cols(estimation_data)
            observed <- get_observed_data(estimation_data, capture_columns)
            estimates <- estimate_n(
                observed,
                n_capture_cols = 2,
                estimator_variant = log_linear_estimator()
            ) |>
                dplyr::mutate(
                    estimate = estimate + n_total,
                    cil = cil + n_total,
                    ciu = ciu + n_total
                )
            return(estimates)
        }))
    }
)

scenario_estimations_ll
```

## Averaged Log Linear Estimates

Similar to the doubly robust estimators, we need to average across all grouped
lists. This is still valid because it is the same population.

```{r averaged-ll}
averaged_ll <- lapply(scenario_estimations_ll, function(scenario) {
    est <- data.frame(
        method = "log_linear",
        avg_n = mean(scenario$estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
        min_cil = min(scenario$cil, na.rm = TRUE),
        max_ciu = max(scenario$ciu, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
    return(est)
})

names(averaged_ll) <- names(combined_scenario_data)
averaged_ll <- bind_rows(averaged_ll, .id = "scenario")


# Combine doubly robust and log-linear
combined <- rbind(averaged, averaged_ll) |> dplyr::arrange(scenario)

combined
```

## Visualization

Now that we've averaged and combined them across estimation methods, we can
visualize the results. This is best done with a bar plot showing the estimated
population size for each scenario and method with error bars corresponding to
the confidence intervals derived from the estimates. A red dashed line indicates
the true population size.

```{r single-simulation-comparison}
n_pop <- 5000 # pre-determined in `simulation_data.qmd`

ggplot(
    combined,
    aes(x = scenario, y = avg_n, fill = method)
) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = n_pop, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    geom_errorbar(
        aes(ymin = min_cil, ymax = max_ciu),
        position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
        width = 0.2
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "Population estimates by scenario and method",
        x = NULL,
        y = "Estimated population size",
        fill = "Method"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# Repeated Simulation Estimation

This follows the same logic as the single-simulation estimation section, except
we repeat the simulation multiple times for each scenario to assess variability.

The first step is to define scenario factories that reproduce the 
data-generating mechanisms with independent seeds. The factories build scenarios
that match a `low_capture`, `mid_capture`, `imbalanced_capture`, and 
`covariate_dependent` capture scenario. Like the single sim, we only use 6 
capture columns and 2 covariates. Additionally, we set it to have 100 replicates
for each scenario and build corresponding seeds to ensure independent 
simulations.

```{r scenario-factories}
n_capture_cols <- 6
n_covariates <- 2

covariate_intercepts <- c(-1.2, -0.8, -1.5, -1.0, -0.5, -1.3)
covariate_coefficients <- rbind(
    capture_1 = c(1.0, -0.5),
    capture_2 = c(0.4, 0.8),
    capture_3 = c(-0.7, 1.2),
    capture_4 = c(0.3, -0.2),
    capture_5 = c(-0.1, 0.4),
    capture_6 = c(0.2, -0.3)
)

cov_dists <- data.frame(
    distribution = c("uniform", "uniform"),
    p1 = c(0, 0),
    p2 = c(1, 1),
    dtype = c("integer", "integer")
)

scenario_factories <- list(
    mid_capture = function(seed) {
        sim_scenario <- simulation_scenario(
            base_scenario = homogeneous_scenario(
                rep(0.5, n_capture_cols),
                n_covariates
            ),
            heterogeneity_scenario = NULL,
            dependence_scenario = NULL
        )
        return(create_scenario_data(
            n_pop = n_pop,
            n_capture_cols = n_capture_cols,
            scenario = sim_scenario,
            seed = seed
        ))
    },
    low_capture = function(seed) {
        sim_scenario <- simulation_scenario(
            base_scenario = homogeneous_scenario(
                rep(0.2, n_capture_cols),
                n_covariates
            ),
            heterogeneity_scenario = NULL,
            dependence_scenario = NULL
        )
        return(create_scenario_data(
            n_pop = n_pop,
            n_capture_cols = n_capture_cols,
            scenario = sim_scenario,
            seed = seed
        ))
    },
    imbalanced_capture = function(seed) {
        sim_scenario <- simulation_scenario(
            base_scenario = homogeneous_scenario(
                c(0.80, 0.35, 0.10, 0.50, 0.05, 0.70),
                n_covariates
            ),
            heterogeneity_scenario = NULL,
            dependence_scenario = NULL
        )
        return(create_scenario_data(
            n_pop = n_pop,
            n_capture_cols = n_capture_cols,
            scenario = sim_scenario,
            seed = seed
        ))
    },
    covariate_capture = function(seed) {
        sim_scenario <- simulation_scenario(
            base_scenario = covariate_scenario(
                cov_dists,
                covariate_intercepts,
                covariate_coefficients
            ),
            heterogeneity_scenario = NULL,
            dependence_scenario = NULL
        )
        return(create_scenario_data(
            n_pop = n_pop,
            n_capture_cols = n_capture_cols,
            scenario = sim_scenario,
            seed = seed
        ))
    }
)

copies <- 100
replicate_seeds <- 20261006 + seq_len(copies)
```

## Repeated Estimation Runner

Again, similar to the single simulation estimation, we estimate the population
size. We add the external loop for each replicate, but otherwise maintain the
same workflow as before. 

Because there are replicates, we also calculate coverage probability, that is,
how often the true population size falls within the estimated confidence
intervals.

:::{.callout-note title="Resusing Capture Groups"}
Because we again utilize 6 capture columns, we can use the same capture group
splits as with the single sim design for consistency across simulations. It does
not need to be recalculated.
:::

```{r repeated-estimation-runner}
run_estimator_replicate <- function(factory, scenario_name, replicate, seed) {
    full_data <- factory(seed)$full_data
    n_total <- nrow(full_data)
    return(bind_rows(lapply(
        names(capture_list_groups),
        function(group_name) {
            estimation_data <- combine_capture_lists(
                full_data,
                capture_list_groups[[group_name]]
            )
            capture_columns <- get_capture_cols(estimation_data)
            observed <- get_observed_data(estimation_data, capture_columns)

            dr_estimates <- estimate_n(
                observed,
                n_capture_cols = 2,
                estimator_variant = doubly_robust_estimator()
            ) |>
                transmute(
                    method,
                    estimate = n,
                    cil = cin.l,
                    ciu = cin.u
                )

            log_linear_estimates <- create_contingency_table(
                estimation_data
            ) |>
                get_observed_data(capture_columns) |>
                estimate_n(
                    n_capture_cols = 2,
                    estimator_variant = log_linear_estimator()
                ) |>
                mutate(
                    estimate = estimate + n_total,
                    cil = cil + n_total,
                    ciu = ciu + n_total,
                    method = "log_linear"
                ) |>
                transmute(method, estimate, cil, ciu)

            return(
                bind_rows(dr_estimates, log_linear_estimates) |>
                    mutate(
                        scenario = scenario_name,
                        replicate = replicate,
                        seed = seed,
                        listpair = group_name,
                        n_total = n_total,
                        bias = estimate - n_total,
                        relative_bias = bias / n_total,
                        coverage = cil <= n_total & ciu >= n_total,
                        interval_width = ciu - cil
                    )
            )
        }
    )))
}

replicate_estimates <- bind_rows(lapply(
    names(scenario_factories),
    function(scenario_name) {
        return(bind_rows(lapply(
            seq_along(replicate_seeds),
            function(replicate) {
                return(run_estimator_replicate(
                    scenario_factories[[scenario_name]],
                    scenario_name,
                    replicate,
                    replicate_seeds[[replicate]]
                ))
            }
        )))
    }
))
```

## Estimation Performance Summary

Average estimates and interval bounds across list pairs within each replicate,
then summarize signed bias, relative bias, estimate variability, empirical
confidence-interval coverage, and interval width by scenario and method.

```{r performance-summary}
replicate_method_estimates <- replicate_estimates |>
    group_by(scenario, replicate, method) |>
    summarise(
        seed = first(seed),
        n_total = first(n_total),
        estimate = mean(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
        cil = min(cil, na.rm = TRUE),
        ciu = max(ciu, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
        bias = estimate - n_total,
        relative_bias = bias / n_total,
        coverage = cil <= n_total & ciu >= n_total,
        interval_width = ciu - cil
    )

replicate_summary <- replicate_method_estimates |>
    group_by(scenario, method) |>
    summarise(
        replicates = n(),
        avg_n = mean(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_n = sd(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
        avg_cil = min(cil, na.rm = TRUE),
        avg_ciu = max(ciu, na.rm = TRUE),
        mean_bias = mean(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_bias = median(bias, na.rm = TRUE),
        rmse = sqrt(mean(bias^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
        coverage = mean(coverage, na.rm = TRUE),
        mean_interval_width = mean(interval_width, na.rm = TRUE),
        interval_width_q05 = quantile(interval_width, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
        interval_width_q95 = quantile(interval_width, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

replicate_summary
```

## Visualizations

Now we do the same visualization for the repeated-estimation results.

```{r performance-visualizations}
ggplot(
    replicate_summary,
    aes(x = scenario, y = avg_n, fill = method)
) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = n_pop, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    geom_errorbar(
        aes(ymin = avg_cil, ymax = avg_ciu),
        position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
        width = 0.2
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "100 Repeated population estimates by scenario and method",
        x = NULL,
        y = "Mean estimated population size",
        fill = "Method"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
